item.content:encoded:
Applications are now open for the Interledger Local Impact Mini-Grants 2026, a global funding programme supporting locally designed projects that advance open payments, digital financial access, financial inclusion, open-source innovation and digital public infrastructure.

The programme recognizes that some of the most effective financial-inclusion initiatives begin at the community level. Local organizers, nonprofit organizations, cooperatives, fintech innovators, researchers and civil-society groups often understand the financial barriers facing their communities better than outside institutions. The initiative therefore provides flexible funding directly to people and organizations capable of designing activities around those local needs.

Selected applicants can receive between USD 500 and USD 3,000 to organize workshops, community conversations, demonstrations, hackdays, research, awareness campaigns, local ecosystem events and other activities connected to open and inclusive payment systems.

Applications opened on 6 July 2026 and are being reviewed on a rolling basis. The final deadline is 11 November 2026 at 11:59 p.m. ET/EDT.

Interledger Local Impact Mini-Grants 2026: Key Information

Programme detail Information
Programme name Interledger Local Impact Mini-Grants 2026
Funding organization Interledger Foundation
Funding amount USD 500–3,000 per selected project
Application opening date 6 July 2026
Application deadline 11 November 2026 at 11:59 p.m. ET/EDT
Review process Rolling review
Project duration Within six months of accepting the funding
Application platform Submittable
Geographic coverage Worldwide, subject to applicable United States sanctions
Priority communities Global South, rural and peri-urban communities with limited access to formal financial services
Eligible applicant types Individuals and registered or unregistered organizations
Previous Interledger experience Not required
Main application documents Application form, two-page concept note, project budget and implementation timeline

What Are the Interledger Local Impact Mini-Grants?

The Interledger Local Impact Mini-Grants provide small and flexible awards for grassroots initiatives focused on open payments and digital financial access.

The programme is built around the idea that local people should have an active role in identifying financial-access problems, convening affected communities and experimenting with appropriate solutions. Rather than prescribing one project model, the Interledger Foundation allows applicants to propose activities based on their community’s circumstances.

Projects may focus on education, research, community engagement, technical experimentation, public awareness, policy discussion or local ecosystem development. A project does not necessarily have to build a new financial product. Nontechnical initiatives such as community workshops, research, storytelling, policy conversations and educational content may also qualify if they clearly connect to open payments or digital financial inclusion.

The programme’s central objective is to help communities:

  • Understand open and interoperable payment systems;
  • Explore barriers to digital financial access;
  • Learn about financial technologies that may improve inclusion;
  • Conduct locally relevant research;
  • Bring together community members, developers, policymakers and financial-sector stakeholders;
  • Experiment with open-payment technologies;
  • Produce knowledge and educational materials;
  • Share local evidence and lessons with the wider Interledger community.

About the Interledger Foundation

The Interledger Foundation is a nonprofit organization working to expand equitable participation in the digital economy. It supports financial-service initiatives, education programmes, community engagement and technologies intended to make payment systems more open and interoperable.

The Foundation works with entrepreneurs, community organizations, governments, educational institutions and technology developers. Its wider vision is to make it easier for people to send and receive digital payments across platforms, currencies and national borders.

Traditional payment networks frequently operate as separate systems. This can make transactions between different providers, ledgers or currencies expensive, slow or inaccessible. The Interledger Protocol is an open protocol designed to enable value to move across independent payment networks. It is not restricted to one company, currency or payment provider.

Applicants do not need to be technical experts in the Interledger Protocol. However, their proposed activities should create opportunities for communities to learn about or engage with open payments, interoperability, digital financial infrastructure or related financial-inclusion issues.

Why the Local Impact Programme Was Created

Financial exclusion is not experienced in exactly the same way in every community. One region may struggle with expensive remittance services, while another may face limited access to bank accounts, weak digital infrastructure, low financial literacy, inaccessible payment platforms or a lack of trust in formal financial institutions.

Local organizations and community practitioners are often well positioned to understand these barriers because they already have trusted relationships, firsthand knowledge and established local networks.

Through the Local Impact Mini-Grants, the Interledger Foundation aims to place resources in the hands of people who can:

  • Identify specific financial-access problems within their communities;
  • Explain open-payment concepts in locally appropriate ways;
  • Convene relevant community members and stakeholders;
  • Create space for discussion and practical experimentation;
  • Build local knowledge about interoperable financial systems;
  • Document lessons that could benefit other communities;
  • Connect local initiatives with a wider global network working on financial inclusion.

The programme is particularly interested in proposals that emerge directly from the communities they intend to serve.

Who Can Apply?

The programme is open to both individuals and organizations. An applicant does not have to be a registered nonprofit or formally incorporated entity.

Eligible applicants include:

  • Individual community leaders;
  • Individual practitioners with concrete project plans;
  • Registered and unregistered community organizations;
  • Nonprofit organizations;
  • Cooperatives;
  • Civil-society organizations;
  • Advocacy and consumer-rights groups;
  • Local fintech startups;
  • Mission-aligned businesses;
  • Social enterprises;
  • Research groups;
  • Open-source communities;
  • Innovation hubs;
  • Hacker spaces;
  • Coworking communities;
  • Incubators and accelerators;
  • Startup communities;
  • Universities and university-linked groups;
  • Fintech and payment-sector communities;
  • Organizations working on Sustainable Development Goals;
  • Groups focused on digital public infrastructure or digital public goods.

Applicants should have a direct connection with the community they propose to serve and a realistic plan for delivering the project.

The official announcement does not state a minimum academic degree, professional certification or age requirement. Formal organizational registration is also not mandatory.

Geographic Eligibility and Priority Communities

Applications are welcomed from around the world. Projects may be proposed from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Oceania and other regions.

For the 2026 cycle, priority will be given to projects serving:

  • Communities in the Global South;
  • Rural communities;
  • Peri-urban communities;
  • Areas with limited access to formal financial services;
  • Regions that have historically been underrepresented in open-payment and financial-technology initiatives.

The Interledger Foundation is incorporated in the United States and must comply with sanctions administered by the United States Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control. Applicants from countries subject to applicable United States sanctions may be ineligible. The Foundation is also prohibited from supporting sanctioned individuals and entities appearing on relevant restricted-party lists unless an authorization or exemption applies.

Applicants who are uncertain about sanctions-related eligibility should contact the Interledger Foundation before preparing a full submission.

How Much Funding Is Available?

Each selected project may receive between:

  • Minimum funding: USD 500
  • Maximum funding: USD 3,000

The amount requested should be proportionate to the proposed activities. Applicants should not automatically request the maximum amount unless their budget demonstrates that the full amount is necessary.

The award is intended primarily for direct project costs rather than an organization’s routine operating expenses.

The published call does not specify the total number of awards available. Because applications are assessed on a rolling basis, early submission is strongly recommended.

What Selected Applicants Will Receive

Successful applicants will receive more than project funding. According to the official programme information, grantees may benefit from:

  • USD 500–3,000 for approved project activities;
  • Flexible support for community-led education and engagement;
  • Access to Interledger educational and technical resources;
  • Opportunities to connect with the wider open-payments community;
  • Exposure to a global network of practitioners working on digital financial access;
  • Opportunities to document and share local findings;
  • Potential connections with other community leaders, developers and organizations.

The programme can therefore help an applicant test a local idea, build community understanding and establish relationships within the international open-payments ecosystem.

Main Areas the Programme Supports

Projects should connect meaningfully with at least one of the programme’s main focus areas.

1. Open Payments and Digital Financial Access

Projects may help communities understand, discuss or experiment with payment systems that are open, accessible and capable of working across different platforms.

Potential topics include:

  • Barriers to receiving digital payments;
  • Access to payment accounts;
  • Cross-border payments and remittances;
  • Payment interoperability;
  • Community understanding of digital financial services;
  • Affordable payment tools for small businesses, creators or underserved populations.

2. Open Source and Open Innovation

Applicants may propose activities that encourage communities to learn about, develop or experiment with open-source technologies.

Eligible formats could include:

  • Open-source workshops;
  • Developer meetups;
  • Community demonstrations;
  • Innovation sprints;
  • Collaborative learning sessions;
  • Technical documentation or educational content.

3. Financial Inclusion and Fintech Ecosystems

Projects may examine how financial technology can improve access for underserved groups or strengthen local financial ecosystems.

Relevant initiatives may involve:

  • Bringing together fintech startups and community organizations;
  • Mapping financial-access barriers;
  • Convening discussions on responsible financial innovation;
  • Raising awareness of inclusive digital-finance solutions;
  • Researching consumer experiences with payment services.

4. Digital Public Infrastructure and Digital Public Goods

Applicants may explore the role of Digital Public Infrastructure and Digital Public Goods in enabling equitable access to services.

Projects could examine:

  • Open digital-payment infrastructure;
  • Public-interest technology;
  • Open standards;
  • Financial infrastructure policy;
  • Connections between digital identity, payments and public services;
  • Community participation in the design of digital systems.

5. Interoperability

Interoperability concerns the ability of different financial systems, providers or technologies to communicate and exchange value.

Projects may help participants understand why disconnected payment systems create barriers and how open standards could support more inclusive financial services.

Eligible Project Activities

The programme supports a broad range of community-led activities.

Community meetings and conversations

Applicants may organize:

  • Neighborhood discussions;
  • Community listening sessions;
  • Roundtable meetings;
  • Fintech community gatherings;
  • Consumer-rights discussions;
  • Conversations about local payment challenges.

Workshops, training and demonstrations

Possible activities include:

  • Introductory workshops on open payments;
  • Digital financial-literacy sessions;
  • Demonstrations of Interledger technologies;
  • Training on digital public infrastructure;
  • Capacity-building sessions for nonprofits or community leaders;
  • Practical sessions for developers, students or fintech practitioners.

Hackdays, sprints and innovation challenges

Funding may support:

  • Hackdays;
  • Design sprints;
  • Innovation challenges;
  • Participatory learning sessions;
  • Small-scale technical experiments;
  • Collaborative problem-solving events.

Research and policy work

Eligible research-related activities may include:

  • Community needs assessments;
  • Financial-access studies;
  • Policy briefs;
  • Publications;
  • Interviews and surveys;
  • Documentation of local payment barriers;
  • Research on fintech ecosystems or consumer experiences.

Storytelling and awareness campaigns

Applicants may develop:

  • Community stories;
  • Case studies;
  • Awareness campaigns;
  • Articles and blog posts;
  • Videos or digital content;
  • Educational materials;
  • Public information resources.

Hands-on experimentation

The official programme factsheet also refers to experimentation with technologies such as the Interledger Test Wallet and Web Monetization.

These activities can be organized independently or in partnership with existing institutions such as universities, innovation hubs, coworking spaces, accelerators, incubators, hacker spaces, open-source groups or civil-society networks.

What Grant Funds Can Cover

Funding must be used for costs directly related to delivering the approved project.

Eligible expenses may include:

  • Venue costs for project events;
  • Workshop and training materials;
  • Community-event expenses;
  • Facilitator compensation connected directly to approved activities;
  • Project-specific organizer stipends;
  • Travel required for project delivery;
  • Local transportation and logistics;
  • Research expenses;
  • Communication and awareness materials;
  • Design and production of educational content;
  • Costs associated with demonstrations or participatory sessions;
  • Documentation and reporting materials.

Applicants should make a clear connection between every budget item and a proposed activity or deliverable.

What the Funding Cannot Cover

The programme does not support:

  • General organizational operating expenses;
  • Routine overhead unrelated to the project;
  • General salary or compensation not tied to direct project delivery;
  • Capital expenditure;
  • Major equipment or long-term asset purchases;
  • Costs that cannot be linked to the proposed activities.

The public guidance lists project-specific facilitator compensation and organizer stipends as eligible while excluding general operating compensation. Applicants should therefore distinguish clearly between a limited, activity-based stipend and an organization’s routine payroll or administrative costs.

Any applicant uncertain about a budget item should seek written clarification from the programme team before submitting.

Application Requirements

Applicants must submit their proposal through the Interledger Foundation’s Submittable portal.

A complete application includes:

  1. A completed online application form;
  2. A two-page concept note;
  3. A project budget;
  4. An implementation timeline;
  5. Key project milestones.

The official programme factsheet confirms that the resource folder contains an application guide, concept-note template, and budget and timeline templates.

What to Include in the Two-Page Concept Note

The concept note should provide a concise but convincing explanation of the project.

A strong concept note should address the following points:

Project background

Explain the financial-access, open-payment or digital-infrastructure issue the project will address.

Target community

Identify the people, organizations or local networks that will participate in or benefit from the project.

Local need

Describe why the issue matters in the proposed community. Use local evidence, observations, examples or data where available.

Proposed activities

Clearly explain what the project will do. Activities should be realistic, specific and appropriate for the requested amount.

Connection to the programme

Demonstrate how the project advances open payments, digital financial access, open-source innovation, financial inclusion, fintech ecosystems, interoperability or Digital Public Infrastructure.

Expected results

Describe the knowledge, participation, outputs or changes expected from the project.

Community involvement

Explain how local participants will contribute to the design, delivery or learning process.

Knowledge sharing

Describe how findings, materials or lessons will be shared with the Interledger community and other stakeholders.

Applicants should avoid filling the concept note with broad claims that are not supported by a practical implementation plan.

Preparing the Project Budget

The budget should be realistic, transparent and directly connected to the project’s activities.

Each budget line should show:

  • The proposed item or expense;
  • The quantity or number of units;
  • The estimated unit cost;
  • The total requested amount;
  • The activity the expense supports;
  • A short justification where necessary.

Applicants should ensure that:

  • The total request falls between USD 500 and USD 3,000;
  • All expenses relate directly to project implementation;
  • Costs are reasonable for the applicant’s location;
  • General operating expenses are excluded;
  • Capital purchases are excluded;
  • Travel and logistics are necessary and proportionate;
  • Facilitator or organizer payments relate to specific project activities;
  • The budget matches the activities described in the concept note.

An inflated or unclear budget is likely to weaken an otherwise promising proposal.

Developing the Timeline and Milestones

Projects must be completed within six months of accepting the award.

The timeline should identify:

  • Project start date;
  • Community outreach and participant recruitment;
  • Preparation of training or event materials;
  • Research or content-development stages;
  • Dates of workshops, meetings or hackdays;
  • Expected completion dates for outputs;
  • Documentation activities;
  • Blog and reporting deadlines;
  • Project closing date.

Milestones should be measurable. Instead of writing “conduct community engagement,” an applicant could identify the number of planned sessions, expected participants and target completion date.

Although projects may run for up to six months, the Foundation states that priority review will be given to initiatives expected to finish before 31 December 2026.

How Applications Will Be Reviewed

Applications are assessed as they are received. Applicants do not need to wait until the final deadline for the review process to begin.

The programme is looking for proposals that demonstrate:

  • A clear and realistic project plan;
  • Direct knowledge of the community being served;
  • A meaningful focus on open payments or digital financial access;
  • Strong potential for community learning and participation;
  • Appropriate and well-justified use of funds;
  • Realistic outcomes for the proposed budget;
  • Willingness to share findings and lessons;
  • Capacity to complete the project within six months;
  • Alignment with the programme’s geographic and inclusion priorities.

The Interledger Foundation says its team will follow up within approximately two weeks of submission. Applicants should not assume that this necessarily guarantees a final funding decision within that period, but they should monitor the email address linked to their Submittable account.

Submitting early may improve the likelihood of receiving an award during the current funding cycle.

Is Previous Interledger Experience Required?

No previous experience with Interledger is required.

However, applicants should demonstrate:

  • Genuine interest in learning about Interledger technologies;
  • Willingness to explore open-payment concepts;
  • A plan for introducing their community to the Interledger ecosystem;
  • Readiness to participate in community learning and knowledge sharing.

Applicants who are new to the subject should review Interledger documentation, educational resources, community discussions and developer materials before preparing their concept note.

Expected Deliverables from Successful Projects

Successful applicants will typically be required to produce two main knowledge-sharing deliverables.

Project introduction blog

This blog should introduce the project, explain the planned activities and describe how the wider community may support or engage with the initiative.

Final summary blog

The final blog should summarize:

  • Activities completed;
  • Number of participants reached;
  • Project outcomes;
  • Key performance information;
  • Participant feedback;
  • Lessons learned;
  • Challenges encountered;
  • Recommendations or possible next steps.

Grantees are also encouraged to submit:

  • Photographs;
  • Event materials;
  • Workshop presentations;
  • Research documentation;
  • Educational resources;
  • Other materials that could help the wider Interledger community learn from the project.

Applicants should incorporate documentation and monitoring into their project plans from the beginning rather than attempting to reconstruct evidence after the activities have ended.

Can More Than One Project from the Same Region Be Funded?

The Foundation may fund multiple projects from the same city or region on a case-by-case basis.

However, it also aims to promote geographic diversity. Proposals from regions and communities that are underrepresented in open-payments work may therefore receive priority.

Applicants should focus on the distinct local need their project addresses rather than assuming that the existence of another project in the same region makes them automatically ineligible.

How to Apply

Applicants should follow these steps:

Step 1: Review the programme information

Read the official call, eligibility guidance and frequently asked questions on the Local Impact Mini-Grants page.

Step 2: Study the supporting resources

Review the Local Impact Mini-Grants Factsheet and the official resource folder.

Step 3: Create a Submittable account

Applicants must create a free account on the application platform. A draft can be saved and completed later.

Step 4: Prepare the concept note

Use the official template and keep the document within the required two-page limit.

Step 5: Prepare the budget and timeline

Provide realistic costs, measurable milestones and a completion schedule of no more than six months.

Step 6: Complete the online application

Answer every required question accurately and ensure that the information matches the uploaded documents.

Step 7: Review the submission

Check project dates, contact details, budget totals, attachments and alignment with the programme’s focus areas.

Step 8: Submit early

Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis. Applicants should not wait until the final deadline if their documents are ready.

Step 9: Monitor email communications

The Foundation will communicate through the email address connected to the applicant’s Submittable account.

If submitted information changes, applicants can request permission to edit their submission.

Important Dates

Stage Date or timeframe
Applications opened 6 July 2026
Review process Rolling
Expected follow-up Approximately two weeks after submission
Final application deadline 11 November 2026 at 11:59 p.m. ET/EDT
Priority completion date Projects expected to finish before 31 December 2026 receive priority review
Maximum project duration Six months from acceptance of the award

Applicants should treat the time displayed on the official application portal as authoritative.

Practical Tips for a Competitive Application

Start with a specific local problem

Do not describe financial exclusion only in global terms. Explain the particular problem facing the proposed community.

Demonstrate community connection

Show that the applicant already understands or works with the people the project intends to serve.

Keep the project proportionate

A USD 500–3,000 award is suitable for a focused activity or small series of activities. Avoid proposing a large programme that cannot realistically be completed with the available resources.

Make participation measurable

State how many workshops, participants, interviews, demonstrations, publications or community sessions are expected.

Explain the open-payments connection

The application should make clear how the activities relate to open payments, interoperability, digital financial access or another stated focus area.

Build documentation into the plan

Assign responsibility for photographs, attendance records, participant feedback, project data and final reporting.

Use a transparent budget

Avoid lump-sum costs without explanations. Show how each expense contributes to delivery.

Use plain language

The project should be understandable to reviewers who may not know the applicant’s local context.

Apply before the final deadline

Rolling review means that waiting until November may reduce the opportunity for funding within the current cycle.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can an individual apply?

Yes. Individual community leaders and practitioners can apply if they have a concrete project plan and a direct connection to the proposed community.

Does an organization have to be registered?

No. Registered and unregistered organizations are eligible.

Is a university degree required?

No minimum academic degree is stated in the published eligibility criteria.

Is there an age limit?

No age restriction is stated in the official call.

Is previous technical experience required?

No. Applicants do not need prior experience with Interledger, although they should be willing to learn and introduce relevant concepts to their communities.

Must the project develop software?

No. Software development is not compulsory. Workshops, community conversations, research, storytelling, awareness campaigns, policy briefs and educational content may also qualify.

Can a research project apply?

Yes. Research, publications and policy briefs are listed among eligible activities, provided they align with the programme’s focus.

Can the funding pay for travel?

Travel and logistics may be covered when they are directly necessary for project delivery.

Can the funding pay organizational salaries?

Routine salaries and general operating compensation are not eligible. A facilitator fee or limited organizer stipend may be included when it is directly tied to approved project activities.

Are capital purchases eligible?

No. Capital expenditure is excluded.

Are applicants from the Global South eligible?

Yes. Projects in the Global South are specifically prioritized, together with rural and peri-urban communities that have limited access to formal financial services.

Can applicants from Pakistan apply?

Yes. The call welcomes applications from any geography, including Pakistan, subject to the Foundation’s sanctions and applicant-screening requirements.

Is there a fixed number of awards?

The public programme information does not state the total number of grants to be awarded.

Is co-funding required?

The public call does not identify a mandatory matching-fund or co-funding requirement.

Contact and Support

Applicants can obtain further information through:

  • Grant information: LIG@interledger.org
  • Eligibility and application questions: programteam@interledger.org
  • Submittable technical support: submittersupport@submittable.com
  • Community support: Interledger Slack, including the #local-impact-grants channel
  • Application portal: 2026 Interledger Local Impact Mini-Grant

Applicants should use the official programme and application pages and should not send sensitive financial information through unofficial channels.

Conclusion

The Interledger Local Impact Mini-Grants 2026 provide an accessible funding opportunity for community leaders, nonprofits, cooperatives, researchers, fintech innovators and civil-society groups working to improve digital financial access.

With funding of USD 500–3,000, the programme is suitable for focused, community-led initiatives such as workshops, hackdays, research, storytelling, awareness campaigns, policy conversations and experiments with open-payment technologies.

One of the programme’s most important features is its accessibility. Individuals and unregistered groups can apply, no university degree or previous Interledger experience is required, and applications are accepted worldwide. What matters most is a concrete project plan, a direct connection to the community, a clear relationship with open payments or financial inclusion, and the ability to produce measurable results within six months.

Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis and will close on 11 November 2026 at 11:59 p.m. ET/EDT. Interested applicants should study the official resources, prepare a concise concept note and transparent budget, and submit as early as possible.

item.content:encoded:
Are you a PhD student looking to gain practical research experience at one of the world’s leading independent policy institutes? The Chatham House PhD Research Placement 2026–2027 offers eligible doctoral researchers an opportunity to join the research community at Chatham House, the Royal Institute of International Affairs, in London.m The placement is designed for aspiring researchers who want to strengthen their research, writing, policy analysis, communication and leadership skills while contributing to research projects addressing some of the world’s most important international challenges. Hosted through the Queen Elizabeth II Academy for Leadership and the Next Generation at Chatham House, the placement combines hands-on research experience with leadership development, access to expert networks, events and the Chatham House library.

The placement will run from 1 October 2026 to 8 January 2027 and will be full-time for three months. The successful candidate will be based at Chatham House’s St James’s Square location in London and will work in a hybrid arrangement, with at least two days per week expected onsite.

About Chatham House

Chatham House, the Royal Institute of International Affairs, is an independent policy institute and world-leading think tank based in London. The institute conducts research and analysis on major international and global policy issues. Its work is intended to help governments, businesses, organizations and the wider public better understand complex global developments and make informed decisions. The Chatham House research community brings together experts working across a broad range of geographical and thematic areas. These include international security, global health, international law, Europe, the United States and North America, among many other fields. For doctoral researchers, this environment can provide an opportunity to see how academic research can be translated into policy-relevant analysis and contribute to discussions taking place among researchers, policymakers, practitioners and other international stakeholders.

About the Queen Elizabeth II Academy

The Queen Elizabeth II Academy for Leadership and the Next Generation is designed to empower aspiring young leaders and researchers to engage with major global challenges and contribute to building a better future. Through this PhD placement, the Academy is seeking to welcome doctoral students into the Chatham House research community. The placement provides an opportunity to experience the working environment of a leading policy institute while developing practical skills that complement doctoral research. In addition to working within a Chatham House research programme, the selected student will participate in the Academy’s Leadership Masterclass Programme throughout the placement.

Who Can Apply?

This is an important eligibility requirement.

The application is only open to PhD students affiliated with one of the following three Doctoral Training Programmes (DTPs):

  • UCL, Bloomsbury and East London Doctoral Training Programme
  • London School of Economics Doctoral Training Programme
  • London Interdisciplinary Social Science Doctoral Training Programme

Applicants should therefore confirm their current PhD affiliation and eligibility through their respective doctoral training programme before preparing an application.

Nationality and Geographic Eligibility

The information provided for this opportunity does not identify a specific nationality, race or continent as the eligibility criterion. Instead, the key restriction is institutional: applicants must be PhD students affiliated with one of the three specified DTPs. Consequently, prospective applicants should not assume that this is a general worldwide PhD opportunity. If you are pursuing a PhD but are not affiliated with one of the three listed programmes, you should carefully check whether you meet the eligibility requirements before applying.

Chatham House Research Programmes Available to Applicants

Applicants may apply to one of five Chatham House research programmes.

These are:

  1. Europe Programme
  2. Global Health Programme
  3. International Law Programme
  4. International Security Programme
  5. US and North America Programme

Each programme has specific research themes and questions that prospective applicants can consider when determining where their research interests best fit.

1. Europe Programme

The Europe Programme focuses on major political, economic, security and strategic developments affecting Europe and its relationship with other parts of the world. Potential research topics include:

The role of dual-use technologies and defence-industrial integration in Europe’s economic resilience

This area examines how technologies that can have both civilian and military applications are affecting Europe’s economic resilience, industrial capabilities and security.

Europe’s evolving defence architecture

Applicants can explore how European states are adapting their defence arrangements and how Europe can balance strategic autonomy with cooperation among allies.

Europe’s engagement with India and the Gulf

Another potential research area examines Europe’s relationships with India and the Gulf, particularly in relation to:

  • Trade
  • Technology
  • Critical minerals
  • Strategic partnerships
  • Emerging international economic relationships

This topic provides an opportunity to explore how Europe is developing new forms of international cooperation in a changing geopolitical environment.

2. Global Health Programme

The Global Health Programme focuses on international health challenges and the policies, institutions and cooperation mechanisms required to address them. Potential areas of research include:

Cooperation on stockpiling medical supplies

Applicants may examine considerations surrounding international cooperation on the stockpiling of medical supplies to strengthen preparedness for future health emergencies. This could involve questions about international coordination, supply chains, preparedness strategies and access to essential medical resources.

Private sector investment in global biosecurity

Another research area concerns the prospects for mobilizing private-sector investment into global biosecurity. This could involve examining how governments, businesses, investors and international institutions can work together to strengthen preparedness against biological risks.

The future of open science cooperation

Applicants can also explore the future of international open science cooperation and how scientific knowledge, research and collaboration can contribute to addressing global challenges.

3. International Law Programme

The International Law Programme examines how international law and multilateral institutions can respond to a rapidly changing global order. Potential research questions include:

Building a new consensus around international rule of law

One potential area asks how a renewed consensus can be developed around the value of:

  • The international rule of law
  • Multilateral institutions
  • International cooperation
  • Rules-based international relations

Adapting international regulation to a changing global order

Another research area considers what modifications may be needed to international regulation as the global system changes. Applicants may explore how international legal frameworks can adapt to emerging political, economic and technological realities while helping guide and stabilize the evolving international system.

4. International Security Programme

The International Security Programme focuses on major developments affecting international security, defence, conflict and geopolitical relations. Potential research areas include:

Changing security landscapes and alliance dynamics

Applicants may examine how states are responding to changing security environments and evolving relationships between allies.

Rearmament and new military technologies

Another area concerns how rearmament and emerging military technologies are changing the way conflicts are fought. This could include research into how technological developments affect military strategy, defence policy and the character of modern conflict.

Peacemaking and safeguarding the international system

Applicants may also examine how states can redefine peacemaking approaches and contribute to safeguarding the international system during periods of geopolitical uncertainty.

5. US and North America Programme

The US and North America Programme examines developments involving the United States, Canada and their relationships with Europe, the UK and the wider international system.Potential research topics include:

America’s evolving role in global affairs

Applicants may explore the changing role of the United States in international affairs and examine the durability and implications of its strategic shifts.

Policy changes in Washington and Ottawa

Another area concerns the implications of political and policy developments in Washington and Ottawa for:

  • The United Kingdom
  • Europe
  • North America
  • Transatlantic relations
  • The wider international system

Transatlantic relations in an era of global recalibration

Applicants may also investigate how relationships across the Atlantic are evolving as global power dynamics and strategic priorities change.

What Will the PhD Placement Involve?

The selected PhD student will become part of a Chatham House research team and contribute to a research project for the duration of the placement. The project could involve a variety of outputs and activities, including a research paper, a series of convenings or another comparable research initiative.

The student may be involved in activities such as:

  • Conducting desk research
  • Carrying out literature reviews
  • Contributing to publications
  • Helping draft research outputs
  • Designing and conducting research interviews
  • Collating research feedback
  • Designing research roundtables
  • Developing and delivering research roundtables
  • Synthesizing discussions from high-level workshops and conferences
  • Monitoring important international developments
  • Preparing research briefs
  • Monitoring specific issues relevant to the programme
  • Collaborating with researchers from other regional and thematic programmes

The placement is therefore intended to provide practical exposure to the full research process rather than limiting the student to a single academic task.

Responding to International Developments

A significant component of the placement will involve supporting the research programme in responding to important international developments. The student may be expected to undertake research, prepare written briefs or monitor developments within the programme’s area of focus. This aspect of the placement can be particularly valuable for doctoral researchers interested in policy research because it requires the ability to respond to emerging developments in a timely and analytically rigorous manner.

Cross-Programme Collaboration

Where appropriate, the student may work with colleagues across Chatham House’s different regional and thematic research areas. This provides an opportunity to identify connections between different areas of research and explore possible avenues for collaboration. For example, an international security issue may have implications for Europe, international law, global health or transatlantic relations. Working across research areas can therefore expose the student to interdisciplinary approaches to international affairs.

Research and Grant Proposal Development

The student may also work with the research team to identify and pursue opportunities for developing research and grant proposals.

With support from the programme, the student may contribute to proposals intended for a range of potential funders, including:

  • Governments
  • Businesses
  • Foundations
  • Other potential funding organizations

This can provide valuable exposure to an aspect of research work that is often different from traditional academic doctoral research: developing projects that respond to funders’ priorities and translating research ideas into fundable proposals.

Project Reporting and Budgets

Where appropriate, the student may gain experience in:

  • Drafting project reports
  • Monitoring projects
  • Reconciling project budgets
  • Supporting broader project-management activities

This can help doctoral researchers understand the administrative and operational dimensions of policy research projects.

Supporting Chatham House Events

The student may also support Chatham House events.

Depending on the needs of the programme, this could include:

  • Identifying potential topics
  • Suggesting speakers
  • Supporting event planning
  • Helping prepare research-related events

This can provide direct exposure to the process of bringing experts, researchers and stakeholders together around major international issues.

Leadership Development Through the Queen Elizabeth II Academy

The placement goes beyond research experience.

During the placement, the successful student will participate in the Queen Elizabeth II Academy’s Leadership Masterclass Programme.

The programme takes place every Thursday and includes:

  • Skills workshops
  • Thematic sessions
  • Leadership training

This component is designed to complement the student’s research responsibilities by developing broader professional and leadership capabilities. For PhD researchers considering careers in policy institutions, international organizations, government, think tanks, academia or related fields, leadership development can be an important part of professional preparation.

Access to Chatham House’s Wider Research Community

The selected student will also gain access to Chatham House’s wider networks, library and events programme. Chatham House hosts a busy schedule of events involving experts from around the world. Participation in this environment can expose the student to discussions involving leading researchers, policymakers and practitioners. The placement therefore offers more than an office-based research experience. It places the student within a broader policy and research ecosystem.

Skills and Qualities Chatham House Is Looking For

Applicants should demonstrate a strong combination of academic research ability, policy interest, communication skills and professional working habits.

1. Strong Research Skills

The student should have strong research skills in a relevant field.

A particularly important ability is the capacity to synthesize complex information.

This means applicants should be able to examine information from different sources, identify the most important findings and communicate them in a clear and structured way.

2. Interest in Foreign Policy and International Affairs

Applicants should demonstrate an interest in foreign policy and international affairs broadly.

Given the nature of the five available research programmes, applicants should be able to demonstrate why their interests align with the research area they are applying to.

3. Excellent Written and Verbal Communication

The placement requires excellent professional communication skills.

Applicants should be able to communicate complex ideas clearly, both in writing and verbally.

This is particularly important in a policy environment, where research findings often need to be communicated to audiences who may not have specialist academic knowledge.

4. Strong Attention to Detail

The student should have excellent attention to detail and the ability to work effectively under tight timeframes.

The placement may involve balancing several responsibilities at the same time, so applicants should demonstrate the ability to prioritize tasks and maintain quality while working to deadlines.

5. Collaborative Working Style

The successful candidate should have a collaborative approach and be capable of building positive working relationships with people at different levels, both within and outside the organization.

Research at a major policy institute frequently involves collaboration among researchers, policy experts, event teams, external partners and other stakeholders.

6. IT Skills

Applicants should have good IT skills and familiarity with the Microsoft Office 365 suite, including:

  • Microsoft Teams
  • Microsoft Word
  • Microsoft Outlook

Familiarity with these tools will help the student contribute effectively to research, communication, meetings, document preparation and collaborative work.

Placement Duration and Location

The placement will run for approximately three months.

Start date: 1 October 2026
End date: 8 January 2027
Duration: 3 months
Working arrangement: Full-time
Location: St James’s Square, London
Work model: Hybrid
Onsite requirement: At least 2 days per week in the London office

Applicants should therefore consider the practical implications of undertaking a full-time placement in London and meeting the required onsite attendance.

Application Deadline

The application deadline is:

Monday, 7 September 2026 at 23:59 GMT.

Applicants should avoid waiting until the final hours to submit their applications. Preparing a strong application can require time, particularly when applicants need to demonstrate how their doctoral research connects with the selected Chatham House programme and proposed research themes.

Important Warning About the Use of AI

Chatham House has issued a specific instruction to applicants regarding artificial intelligence.

Applicants are asked not to use AI for their application.

The organization wants to hear the applicant’s genuine answers and states that it can distinguish between authentic responses and AI-generated applications.

According to the application guidance, using AI creates a risk that an application may be disqualified.

Applicants should therefore ensure that their application reflects their own experiences, research interests, ideas, writing and understanding.

Rather than attempting to generate application answers with AI, applicants should focus on presenting their genuine academic and professional background and explaining clearly why they are interested in the selected Chatham House research programme.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Eligible PhD students can strengthen their preparation by carefully considering the relationship between their doctoral research and their chosen Chatham House research programme.

Before applying, applicants should:

  1. Confirm their DTP eligibility.
    Make sure they are affiliated with one of the three specified Doctoral Training Programmes.
  2. Select one research programme carefully.
    Applicants may apply to one of the five available Chatham House programmes, so their choice should be well aligned with their academic and research interests.
  3. Study the proposed research themes.
    Review the topics listed under the selected programme and identify where your existing research experience and interests connect.
  4. Review the placement responsibilities.
    Understand that the role involves research, writing, interviews, events, collaboration, research monitoring and potentially grant proposal development.
  5. Demonstrate research ability.
    Be prepared to show that you can analyze and synthesize complex information.
  6. Show policy relevance.
    Explain how your academic interests connect to foreign policy and international affairs.
  7. Highlight communication skills.
    Policy research requires the ability to communicate complex findings to different audiences.
  8. Demonstrate collaboration.
    Give genuine examples of working effectively with others where relevant.
  9. Consider the practical requirements.
    The placement is full-time and hybrid, with at least two days per week onsite in London.
  10. Use your own words.
    Because Chatham House specifically warns applicants against using AI in their applications, applicants should ensure that their submitted responses genuinely represent their own thinking and writing.

Keep a Copy of the Job Description

item.content:encoded:
GIZ Data Governance offers specialised online certificate courses through the atingi digital learning platform, providing learners and professionals with an opportunity to strengthen essential skills in data governance, Africa’s data economy, digital policy, cross-border data flows, data localisation, trust, accountability and responsible data value creation.

The courses are provided by GIZ 1740 DataCipation and are particularly relevant to policymakers, regulators, public-sector professionals, IT representatives supporting policy teams, non-technical practitioners and learners interested in building careers in African data governance and digital policy.

Three courses highlighted under the From Policy to Data Value Creation learning offering include:

  1. The African Data Economy in the Global Context
  2. Guardians of Trust
  3. Unleashing Data Value: From Data Localisation to Cross-Border Data Flows

Each course has an estimated learning duration of approximately 1.5 hours and provides a certificate after assessment.

The courses form part of the broader From Policy to Data Value Creation learning offering and are particularly relevant for people working or seeking to work at the intersection of data, governance, regulation, digital transformation and public policy in Africa.

About the GIZ Data Governance Courses on atingi

Data has become an increasingly important resource for governments, businesses, researchers, development organisations and communities. However, creating value from data involves much more than simply collecting information.

Questions surrounding who can access data, where information can be stored, how it can move across borders, which safeguards should apply, how institutions cooperate, and how citizens and stakeholders can participate in governance decisions have become central to Africa’s digital development.

These GIZ DataCipation courses introduce learners to different dimensions of those challenges.

Rather than treating data governance as an exclusively technical subject, the courses examine its broader societal, regulatory, institutional and economic dimensions.

This makes the learning opportunity particularly relevant to policymakers and other professionals who may not be data scientists or software engineers but whose work involves decisions about digital policy, governance, regulation, institutional coordination or public-sector transformation.

The training also demonstrates how African countries and institutions can play an active role in shaping the continent’s data agenda instead of simply adapting to global data systems and standards created elsewhere.

Why Africa’s Data Economy Matters

Africa’s digital transformation is generating growing quantities of data across governments, businesses, financial systems, telecommunications networks, healthcare systems, agriculture, education, infrastructure and other sectors.

However, data only produces meaningful value when appropriate systems allow it to be accessed, shared, combined and reused responsibly.

This creates several important policy questions.

For example:

  • How should data move between institutions within the same country?
  • Under what circumstances should data be allowed to move across national borders?
  • What safeguards should exist when data is shared?
  • How can governments preserve sovereignty while participating in regional and global data ecosystems?
  • How can African countries cooperate on common data-governance principles?
  • How can institutions build public trust in the way data is collected and used?
  • How can stakeholders participate meaningfully in data-governance processes?
  • What role should accountability play when data is exchanged?
  • How can combining local and regional datasets generate additional economic or public value?

The three courses approach these issues from complementary perspectives.

Course 1: The African Data Economy in the Global Context

The African Data Economy in the Global Context examines how Africa’s data economy connects local circumstances with regional and global data systems.

The course emphasises the importance of effective data governance as part of sustainable development and explores Africa’s position within the wider global data ecosystem.

One of its central ideas is that Africa should not be viewed only as a participant in international data systems. African governments, institutions and stakeholders can also actively shape the rules, principles and priorities governing the continent’s data future.

What Does The African Data Economy in the Global Context Cover?

Participants explore the relationship between local, continental and global data systems while considering why cooperation between countries matters.

The course uses real-world cases and African policy frameworks to demonstrate how data governance operates in practice.

Particular attention is given to:

  • Africa’s continental data agenda;
  • regional and international data systems;
  • cross-border data flows;
  • cooperation between countries and institutions;
  • African data-governance frameworks;
  • principles supporting trusted data sharing;
  • the creation of public value from data;
  • economic value creation;
  • local and regional data integration; and
  • Africa’s ability to shape its own data agenda.

The programme therefore gives participants a wider perspective on data governance beyond the policies of an individual institution or country.

Learning Outcomes for The African Data Economy in the Global Context

By completing the course, learners should be able to:

  1. Describe the main idea behind Africa’s continental data agenda and explain why cooperation surrounding data across national borders is important.
  2. Identify important African data-governance frameworks and understand their basic purposes.
  3. Explain how combining local and regional data can create value, including through examples drawn from Gabon and Kenya.
  4. Recognise governance principles that support trusted cross-border data sharing.

These outcomes can be particularly valuable to professionals whose work increasingly requires them to understand how domestic policy interacts with continental and international digital developments.

How Long Does The African Data Economy in the Global Context Course Take?

The estimated duration is:

1.5 hours

This relatively short format makes the course accessible to working professionals who may want to strengthen their understanding of the subject without committing to a lengthy academic programme.

Certificate for The African Data Economy in the Global Context

A certificate is available after assessment.

Participants should therefore expect to complete the required assessment associated with the course to obtain certification.

Publication Date

The supplied course information states that The African Data Economy in the Global Context was published on 12 March 2026.

APPLY NOW

Course 2: Guardians of Trust

The second course, Guardians of Trust, turns attention toward participation, legitimacy, accountability and stakeholder cooperation in data governance.

Effective data governance cannot depend entirely on technical rules or regulations. Institutions also need the confidence and participation of the people and organisations affected by decisions about data.

The course consequently explores how participatory approaches to data governance can strengthen trust, legitimacy and accountability across Africa’s evolving digital environment.

What Does Guardians of Trust Cover?

Using African cases and governance practices, learners examine how engagement and cooperation can contribute to more effective and resilient data-governance systems.

The programme focuses particularly on the importance of:

  • stakeholder engagement;
  • participatory data governance;
  • inclusive governance mechanisms;
  • accountability;
  • legitimacy;
  • public trust;
  • institutional cooperation;
  • multi-stakeholder approaches;
  • public-interest considerations;
  • innovation; and
  • resilient data-governance systems.

The course highlights an important tension in contemporary digital governance: institutions need governance arrangements capable of protecting the public interest while still allowing innovation and responsible data use to develop.

Collaboration is presented as an important part of achieving that balance.

Why Participatory Data Governance Is Important

Data-governance decisions can affect many different groups.

Government departments, regulators, businesses, technology providers, civil society organisations, researchers and members of the public may have different priorities and concerns.

A governance system that does not sufficiently account for relevant stakeholders can encounter challenges surrounding legitimacy, public confidence and implementation.

Participatory approaches can help institutions better understand those competing interests and create governance mechanisms that are more inclusive and accountable.

For policymakers and regulators, this means that successful data governance is not simply about writing rules. It can also involve creating mechanisms through which stakeholders can contribute, institutions can cooperate and decision-makers can remain accountable.

Guardians of Trust Learning Outcomes

By the end of the course, participants should be able to:

  1. Understand the main idea behind Africa’s continental data agenda and why cooperation on data across borders matters.
  2. Identify important African data-governance frameworks and understand their fundamental purposes.
  3. Explore how combining local and regional information can generate value, including through examples involving Kenya and Gabon.
  4. Recognise governance principles supporting trusted data sharing between countries.

These learning outcomes provide participants with both policy context and practical examples for understanding the governance structures surrounding Africa’s developing data economy.

How Long Is the Guardians of Trust Course?

The stated course duration is:

1.5 hours

Does Guardians of Trust Provide a Certificate?

Yes. According to the supplied course information, participants can receive a certificate after assessment.

Learners seeking certification should therefore ensure they complete the required assessment rather than only reviewing the learning materials.

Guardians of Trust Publication Date

The supplied information gives the publication date as:

12 April 2026

APPLY NOW

Course 3: Unleashing Data Value: From Data Localisation to Cross-Border Data Flows

The third course is titled Unleashing Data Value: From Data Localisation to Cross-Border Data Flows.

This course concentrates specifically on the journey that data takes through different systems and examines where value can be created as information moves locally and internationally.

It explores data flows beginning within individual countries and continuing to exchanges taking place across national and regional borders.

A major theme of the course is that governance matters at every stage of this process.

Understanding Data Localisation and Cross-Border Data Flows

Data does not automatically generate value simply because it exists.

How information is governed can influence:

  • who can access it;
  • how it can be reused;
  • whether institutions can share it;
  • where it can move;
  • what safeguards apply;
  • who is accountable for its use; and
  • whether different systems and institutions can cooperate effectively.

The course examines how decisions made throughout the data lifecycle influence access, reuse and value creation.

It also explores the relationship between strong domestic data governance and the ability of countries to participate effectively in trusted cross-border data exchanges.

Local Data Governance as the Foundation for Wider Data Sharing

One of the important ideas addressed by the course is that effective international or regional data sharing depends partly on what happens at the local level.

Strong local data governance can provide a foundation for trusted and scalable data use.

Several factors can influence whether data moves effectively within a country, including:

  • governance structures;
  • standards;
  • institutional coordination;
  • accountability;
  • appropriate safeguards;
  • clarity of purpose; and
  • alignment between relevant institutions and frameworks.

If these underlying conditions are weak, scaling data sharing across borders can become considerably more complicated.

Cross-Border Data Flows Are Governed Pathways

The course also challenges the idea that cross-border data flows should be understood as purely automatic or technical processes.

Instead, Africa’s approach can involve treating them as governed pathways.

For data to move responsibly across borders, appropriate conditions may need to exist.

These include:

  1. Purpose – There should be clarity regarding why information is being shared and what the exchange is intended to achieve.
  2. Safeguards – Appropriate protections need to accompany the movement and use of data.
  3. Accountability – Institutions and actors involved in data exchanges need appropriate responsibilities and accountability mechanisms.
  4. Alignment – Policies, systems or institutional approaches may require sufficient alignment to facilitate responsible cooperation.
  5. Regional coordination – Cross-border exchanges can require cooperation that extends beyond individual national institutions.

The course therefore places value creation alongside other important considerations such as trust and sovereignty.

Learning Outcomes for Unleashing Data Value

After completing Unleashing Data Value: From Data Localisation to Cross-Border Data Flows, learners should be able to:

  1. Understand the data lifecycle and identify where value can be created as data moves through different systems.
  2. Identify factors enabling or constraining local data flows, including governance, standards and institutional coordination.
  3. Analyse the relationship between domestic data governance and cross-border data sharing.
  4. Evaluate the conditions necessary for responsible and trusted cross-border data flows, including purpose, safeguards, accountability and alignment.

These competencies are particularly useful for professionals who need to understand not only whether data can be shared but also the governance conditions under which such sharing can take place responsibly.

Course Duration and Certification

The stated duration for Unleashing Data Value: From Data Localisation to Cross-Border Data Flows is:

1.5 hours

Participants can also obtain a certificate after assessment.

APPLY NOW

Who Are These GIZ Data Governance Courses Designed For?

Across the three courses, the intended audience is centred on professionals working at the intersection of data and governance across Africa.

The programmes are particularly relevant to entry- and mid-level professionals, including IT representatives whose work supports policy teams.

The courses may be especially useful for:

  • Policymakers dealing with digital transformation, data or technology policy;
  • Government regulators;
  • Public-sector professionals;
  • IT representatives supporting policy and governance teams;
  • Professionals who already possess foundational knowledge of data governance and want greater regional or international context;
  • Non-technical professionals who need to understand the societal implications of data;
  • Practitioners interested in regulatory aspects of data governance;
  • Professionals interested in institutional approaches to data;
  • Learners considering careers in African data governance; and
  • People interested in pursuing careers related to digital policy.

Importantly, these courses are not presented as highly technical programmes intended exclusively for programmers, data scientists or engineers.

Their focus extends into policy, institutions, governance, regulation and society, making them potentially valuable for professionals whose responsibilities involve making or supporting decisions about data rather than building the underlying technology.

What Skills and Knowledge Can Participants Develop?

Taken together, the three courses provide learners with an opportunity to build a broader understanding of Africa’s data-governance environment.

Participants can explore several interconnected areas.

1. Africa’s Continental Data Agenda

Learners can develop a clearer understanding of Africa’s emerging continental approach to data and why regional cooperation is becoming increasingly important.

2. African Data-Governance Frameworks

The courses introduce participants to important frameworks and help them understand their basic purposes within the wider African data ecosystem.

3. Cross-Border Data Cooperation

Participants explore why information may need to move between countries and what governance principles can make those exchanges more responsible and trustworthy.

4. Data Value Creation

The courses examine how information can generate economic and public value, particularly when local and regional data can be combined or responsibly reused.

5. Trust and Accountability

Participants can strengthen their understanding of why trust, institutional accountability and legitimacy are fundamental components of sustainable data governance.

6. Stakeholder Participation

Learners examine how inclusive and multi-stakeholder mechanisms can improve governance and help balance innovation with the public interest.

7. Data Localisation

Participants can explore local data flows and the governance conditions affecting how information is accessed, used and exchanged within countries.

8. Data Lifecycle Governance

The training considers how decisions made throughout the lifecycle of data can affect access, reuse, sharing and ultimately the value generated from information.

9. Data Sovereignty

The programmes place cross-border cooperation within the wider discussion about sovereignty, demonstrating that international data sharing and national interests need to be considered together.

Kenya and Gabon as Practical African Examples

The supplied course descriptions specifically reference examples involving Kenya and Gabon.

These examples are used to help participants understand how combining local and regional data can create value.

This practical approach is important because data governance can otherwise appear highly abstract.

By examining African cases, participants can connect concepts such as regional data cooperation, trusted sharing and value creation with situations grounded in the continent’s own institutional and policy environment.

Course Provider: GIZ 1740 DataCipation

The provider listed for the courses is GIZ 1740 DataCipation.

The course pages also identify Germany’s Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development and the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ).

The courses are delivered through atingi, the digital learning platform through which learners can access course materials and enrol in the programmes.

Certification After Assessment

A significant feature of all three courses is the availability of a certificate after assessment.

The supplied information does not state that certificates are awarded merely for opening or viewing the courses. Learners should therefore complete the relevant course requirements and assessment to qualify for the certificate.

For professionals developing careers in data governance, public policy or digital transformation, certificates can also provide evidence of continued professional learning in specialised subject areas.

How Much Time Is Required?

Each of the three highlighted courses has an estimated duration of approximately 1.5 hours.

Completing all three would therefore represent approximately 4.5 hours of stated course duration, although the actual amount of time an individual learner spends may vary depending on their learning pace and assessment requirements.

The relatively short format could make the courses particularly convenient for busy public-sector professionals and policymakers.

How to Enrol in the Courses

The course pages indicate that people viewing the programmes as guests need to enrol before taking the courses.

The general process is:

  1. Visit the relevant course page on the atingi platform.
  2. Select the option to enrol.
  3. Existing atingi users should log in to their accounts where required.
  4. People who do not already have an account will need to register on the platform.
  5. Enrol in the selected course.
  6. Work through the course materials.
  7. Complete the required assessment.
  8. Meet the applicable requirements to obtain the course certificate.

Learners interested in the wider subject area should also explore the From Policy to Data Value Creation learning offering, under which these courses are listed.

Is There an Application Deadline?

No enrolment or application deadline is stated in the supplied course information.

Prospective learners should therefore avoid assuming that a particular closing date applies unless one is displayed during the enrolment process or subsequently announced by the course provider.

The first course, The African Data Economy in the Global Context, has a stated publication date of 12 March 2026, while Guardians of Trust has a stated publication date of 12 April 2026.

No publication date was included in the supplied information for Unleashing Data Value: From Data Localisation to Cross-Border Data Flows.

Course Licensing and Reuse of Materials

The supplied information states that the course materials are licensed under CC BY-SA unless stated differently within the course.

Learners or organisations interested in reusing course materials should therefore pay attention to the specific licensing information and any exceptions displayed within individual course resources.

Disclosure of Artificial Intelligence Use in Course Development

The course provider also includes a disclosure explaining how artificial intelligence was incorporated into the content-development process.

According to the disclosure, the written course materials were created by Akryl Digital Agency using trusted sources, including official partner sources and other materials supplied by stakeholders.

The disclosure states that ChatGPT 5.2 was subsequently used to reword and summarise material while seeking to preserve factual accuracy and make the content more appropriate for e-learning.

AI was also used to support activities such as:

  • Generating and reflecting on ideas;
  • Drafting module structures; and
  • Refining didactic methods.

The stated period during which the tool was used was October 2025 to February 2026.

Questions concerning the role of AI in developing the materials can be directed to the course-design contact provided by the publisher at design@akryl.consulting.

Course Contact Information

The course contact listed across the supplied course information is:

Lorretta Kade
Email: lorretta.kade@giz.de

Prospective learners with questions that are not addressed on the course platform may use the listed contact details to seek additional information from the provider.

Why These Courses May Be Valuable for African Digital Policy Professionals

Africa’s digital transformation increasingly requires professionals who can understand technology through the lens of governance, institutions, regulation and public value.

Data-sharing systems can create significant opportunities, but those opportunities also introduce questions surrounding responsibility, sovereignty, accountability, safeguards and trust.

The three GIZ DataCipation courses approach these challenges from interconnected perspectives.

The African Data Economy in the Global Context helps participants understand Africa’s position within wider regional and global data ecosystems.

Guardians of Trust highlights the human and institutional dimensions of governance, particularly participation, legitimacy, accountability and stakeholder cooperation.

Unleashing Data Value: From Data Localisation to Cross-Border Data Flows examines how data moves and how governance can influence value creation from the local level through to cross-border exchanges.

Together, these subjects can help professionals develop a more rounded understanding of what effective data governance requires.

Conclusion

The GIZ DataCipation data-governance courses available through atingi provide a focused learning opportunity for policymakers, regulators, public-sector professionals, IT representatives supporting policy teams and other learners interested in Africa’s evolving digital and data-policy landscape.

Through The African Data Economy in the Global Context, Guardians of Trust, and Unleashing Data Value: From Data Localisation to Cross-Border Data Flows, participants can explore the relationship between local data governance, continental cooperation and the global data economy.

The courses address critical themes including cross-border data flows, data localisation, trusted data sharing, stakeholder participation, accountability, institutional coordination, sovereignty and the creation of economic and public value from data.

Each course requires approximately 1.5 hours according to the supplied information and offers a certificate after assessment, providing a relatively accessible pathway for professionals seeking targeted learning without committing to a long-term programme.

Most importantly, the training presents Africa not simply as a region responding to global digital developments, but as an active participant in defining its own approach to data governance, cooperation and value creation.

There is no application or enrolment deadline stated in the information provided. Interested learners can therefore explore the courses through the atingi platform, register for an account if necessary, enrol in the relevant programme and complete the assessment requirements for certification.
